idiom_name: @Injectable constructor injection resolved from a module's providers array
implementation_notes: NestJS marks classes @Injectable and resolves constructor parameters from the module's providers array, where each entry binds a token to a class, value or factory (useClass/useValue/useFactory) and @Inject(token) disambiguates non-class tokens; Angular's DI and InversifyJS work the same way, reading the design:paramtypes metadata emitted by emitDecoratorMetadata. What replaces the injector is the framework's runtime container plus module registration. Without decorators, plain constructor parameters or deps-object factory functions with a composition root are the type-safe default.
pitfalls: Without emitDecoratorMetadata/reflect-metadata the design:paramtypes metadata is empty and injection fails at run time with obscure errors.
Circular imports break decorator metadata (the class is undefined when the decorator runs) - use forwardRef or restructure.
Builders such as esbuild/swc without the metadata plugin silently break framework DI - keep tsc or add the plugin.

variants.name: InversifyJS framework-agnostic container
variants.implementation_notes: InversifyJS declares bindings imperatively - container.bind<OrderRepository>(TYPES.Repo).to(SqlOrderRepository).inSingletonScope() - marks classes @injectable(), and resolves class-identifier or Symbol/string tokens with @inject. It only needs reflect-metadata when class identifiers are used directly, so Symbol tokens are recommended for circular imports and multi-implementation modules. What replaces hand-wiring is the container's binding registry; choose it when the app should not adopt a whole framework but wants a typed container with scopes and modules.
pitfalls: Import reflect-metadata once at the entry point and enable the TS decorator options, or @injectable registers nothing.
Circular dependencies need lazyInject or Symbol tokens; direct class identifiers are undefined at decorator time.

variants.name: Typed deps objects with a composition root (no decorators)
variants.implementation_notes: Without decorators or a container, TypeScript injects by passing: services take a deps object or parameter list typed by interfaces, factory functions return implementations closed over their dependencies, and one composition root builds the graph. Structural typing means any object with the right shape is a valid implementation, so tests pass fakes directly and no reflect-metadata, tsconfig flags or framework is needed. This is the pragmatic default for libraries, CLIs and serverless code; adopt a container only when the graph or the lifetime matrix gets large.
pitfalls: Interface types vanish at run time, so a wrong implementation fails late unless the composition root or a contract test pins behaviour.
Threading the deps object through many layers can become a parameter-object by another name - keep factories at the boundaries.
